insights.title: Preserve parser and collection state together
insights.trigger: Parser cursors, token streams, lambda environments, hash buckets, set membership, or sparse table semantics are repaired together.
insights.goal: Keep state shared across helper calls without turning absent keys, empty buckets, or environments into local-only approximations.
insights.constraint: Do not reset parser cursors, hash buckets, set membership, or environments inside helpers that C keeps shared for the public operation.
insights.risk: A broad repair can improve one parser or collection case while regressing another by applying the wrong shortcut outside its state model.
insights.guidance: Use C helpers to identify the state carrier for each domain: parser cursor/token arrays, environment or definition tables, bucket occupancy, key equality, and deleted/empty sentinels. Preserve absent-key behavior explicitly rather than treating default values as present entries.

insights.title: Close parser entrypoints over reachable local helpers
insights.trigger: A public parser entrypoint sees private parse helpers, parser context methods, or recursive-descent stages that are still stubs.
insights.goal: Make the public parse call run complete parser logic without reaching unfinished module-level helpers.
insights.constraint: Do not implement an entrypoint as only context construction plus a call to a bare parse helper when that helper or its context methods are still unimplemented in the displayed shared items.
insights.risk: The crate can compile and the entrypoint body can look tidy, but runtime tests panic immediately when execution reaches a dangling parser helper.
insights.guidance: If the listed parse_regex/parse_term/parse_factor/parse_atom-style helpers or ParseContext methods are stubs, keep the full recursive-descent helper chain inside the public entrypoint as nested local functions over one shared cursor, or patch the helper impl only when that shared item is explicitly repairable. The entrypoint should consume the same cursor, construct AST/NFA/state objects locally, return parser errors instead of panicking, and check end-of-input after the local parse completes.

insights.title: Complete automaton minimization remap loops
insights.trigger: A deterministic automaton builder merges equivalent states, rebuilds a compact state list, or recomputes transition targets after minimization.
insights.goal: Return a fully remapped automaton with complete transition and terminal-state logic.
insights.constraint: Do not leave placeholder local variables, partially written loops, or a first pass that reads remapped indexes before every survivor and representative has a stable new index.
insights.risk: The translation can build most of the automaton correctly but fail compilation or tests at the final minimization step because merged transitions still point at old indexes or an unfinished self-index loop remains.
insights.guidance: When merging equivalent states, first compute each old state's representative, then assign new indexes to all surviving representatives, and only then build the compact state vector. Fill every transition through the representative-to-new-index map. Set per-state terminal or self-loop flags with an enumerate loop over the final vector, not with a placeholder self-index variable or a separate unfinished pass.

insights.title: Iterate byte alphabets without overflowing u8 endpoints
insights.trigger: A parser, regex engine, automaton, DFA/NFA serializer, or symbol-set formatter iterates over all byte values or rebuilds transitions for every character.
insights.goal: Cover exactly byte values 0 through 255 while keeping transition indexes valid after serialization and deserialization.
insights.constraint: Do not write an exclusive Rust range with an out-of-range u8 endpoint such as 0..256u8, and do not let missing transitions serialize as usize::MAX unless the reader explicitly maps that sentinel.
insights.risk: A repair can fix automaton logic conceptually but fail compilation on an overflowing u8 literal, or it can compile and then deserialize usize::MAX as an invalid target state.
insights.guidance: When the C code loops over the full unsigned char alphabet, use 0u16..=255 and cast inside the loop, or use 0..=u8::MAX. For transition tables, choose one sentinel convention for absent targets and use it symmetrically in serialize and deserialize; if the Rust reader validates target < states.len(), map absent targets to None before validation instead of decoding -1 as usize::MAX. When remapping minimized states, fill every byte transition through the representative/new-index map before writing the serialized table.

insights.title: Index NFA wrapper states in the vector that owns them
insights.trigger: A regex parser or automaton builder wraps an existing NFA for star, plus, optional, concatenation, alternation, padding, or complement operations.
insights.goal: Keep epsilon targets valid while adding synthetic start/final states around an existing state vector.
insights.constraint: Do not index the original pre-wrapper state vector with indexes that already include a prepended synthetic start offset. Do not leave epsilon targets pointing past states.len().
insights.risk: The parser can build simple NFAs but panic on repeat operators because old_final + 1 is used before the shifted states have been inserted into the new vector.
insights.guidance: Choose one indexing frame for each wrapper operation. If mutating the original vector before inserting a new start state, use original indexes such as old_final = nfa.final_ and write nfa.states[old_final].epsilon*. If building a new vector that starts with a synthetic state and then shifted old states, use shifted indexes only after the new vector exists, for example states[old_final + 1].epsilon*. Set the new final index to 1 + old_len only after accounting for the prepended start. After star/plus/optional/union/concat construction, every target, epsilon0, epsilon1, initial, and final index must be strictly less than states.len().

insights.title: Complete DFA decompilation with state elimination
insights.trigger: A regex or automaton public decompile/uncompile path is still a stub, or repairs mention local arrow/precedence helpers while converting a DFA back to a pattern.
insights.goal: Return a parseable regular expression for the DFA instead of leaving the decompile path as a placeholder.
insights.constraint: Do not leave `unimplemented!()`, `todo!()`, `panic!()`, or a dummy empty result in any public decompile path that the tests call after compile/serialize/uncompile. Do not roll back a verbose but complete decompile implementation to a compiling stub during repair. Do not rely on moving local helper records out of a table if the same record must be reused for multiple bypass paths.
insights.risk: The automaton can compile, match, serialize, and uncompile correctly but still fail when the test performs DFA -> regex -> parse -> compile. Repairs often then fail compilation because local Arrow-like records are moved, cloned without a Clone implementation, or compared by enum casts with precedence errors.
insights.guidance: Implement a local state-elimination algorithm: create an extra sentinel start/final slot, add epsilon arrows from the sentinel to the real initial state and from accepting states to the sentinel, group all byte transitions between each state pair into a symbol-set label, then repeatedly eliminate a real state by composing incoming, self-loop, and outgoing arrows and unioning with any existing arrow. Represent missing arrows explicitly with Option or an empty helper constructor. If a local helper struct or enum is stored in a Vec/table and reused, derive or implement Clone for that local helper; if precedence ordering is needed, derive PartialOrd/Ord on the local enum or parenthesize every enum cast comparison. Parenthesize comparisons such as `(prec as u8) < other_prec as u8`. Keep full-byte loops in a non-overflowing form such as `0u16..256` or `0..=u8::MAX`. A compile fix for this callable must preserve a real returned regex; if ownership or precedence errors are hard, simplify the labels or clone helper records, but never replace the body with `unimplemented!()`/`todo!()` or an empty string just to satisfy the compiler.

insights.title: Make mutating sequence entrypoints change length and order
insights.trigger: A public vector/list/splice/remove/swap-remove callable mutates a sequence by start index, count, or capacity.
insights.goal: Preserve the caller-visible length and element order changes instead of returning a successful no-op.
insights.constraint: Do not leave a mutating entrypoint with an empty body, a dummy success return, or only a capacity check when the C operation removes, shifts, swaps, truncates, or compacts elements. Do not add Copy or Clone bounds to an unconstrained public generic mutator just to move elements.
insights.risk: The crate can compile and many independent vector helpers can pass, but splice-style tests still see the original length because the translated mutator did nothing. A repair that uses slice::copy_within on Vec<T> can also fail compilation because copy_within requires T: Copy.
insights.guidance: Translate the mutation itself. For ordered splice/remove operations, clamp the removed range to the current length and drain or shift elements so survivors keep their relative order. For swap-splice/swap-remove operations on an unconstrained Vec<T>, do not use copy_within, clone, or a new trait bound. Use swaps between the removal range and the original tail, or move values through drain/collect/append so ownership is transferred. A safe pattern is: remember the original length, clamp count, swap each destination slot with the corresponding slot from the original tail when order is irrelevant, then truncate to original_len - count. Compute the tail source from the original length before removal, and never remove the target range first and then insert tail elements at the old start index without clamping; after any drain/truncate, the insertion or overwrite index must be at most the current length. If the target range touches or overlaps the tail, move only the actually available tail elements and finish by truncating. Keep out-of-range start/count behavior aligned with the C code, and make capacity helpers separate from logical length changes.

insights.title: Emit both directed contact force updates
insights.trigger: A contact loop accumulates normal and tangential pair forces for two endpoints and stores previous-force state in pair-indexed arrays.
insights.goal: Make every contact visibly update both directed pair slots and both endpoint force accumulators.
insights.constraint: Do not translate a two-endpoint contact as a single directed update plus a comment about C semantics. Do not rely on one equal-and-opposite force write to stand in for the reverse matrix slot or the first endpoint's accumulator. Do not leave the reverse direction hidden behind a helper whose arguments are passed by value.
insights.risk: The code compiles and one endpoint may move, but tests or callers that inspect the other endpoint or the reverse previous-force cell observe zero force because the public loop never executed that directed update.
insights.guidance: In the public contact loop, build an explicit two-call or two-block shape. First compute the forward direction from source endpoint A to destination endpoint B, read and write the `A * count + B` normal/tangent history slot, and add the signed normal plus tangential contribution to B's output force. Then compute the reverse direction from B to A, with the normal vector negated, relative velocity order swapped, destination material/properties taken from A, the history slot changed to `B * count + A`, and the output force write changed to A's accumulator. The reverse block must repeat the same clamping and friction-limit order as the forward block; it is not a cosmetic mirror or a post-processing subtraction. If a helper cannot mutate the previous normal force, previous tangential force, and destination output vector in place, inline the arithmetic twice in the public loop. A correct patch should make both matrix indexes and both endpoint output writes obvious in the generated Rust.

insights.title: Update both pairwise contact output slots
insights.trigger: A pairwise collision/contact/force loop writes normal, tangent, previous-state, or resultant force arrays through output parameters.
insights.goal: Preserve the C side effects for both endpoints and both matrix directions of each pairwise interaction.
insights.constraint: Do not compute only one direction, do not leave either endpoint's resultant force as zero, and do not share one previous-force slot for both endpoints when the C code indexes a matrix by source and destination. Do not stop after writing only `forces[dst]`, `forces[p2]`, or one `normal_forces[src * n + dst]` slot. Do not delegate the real update to a helper whose signature takes previous force or output vectors by value or immutable reference.
insights.risk: The numeric helper can compile and simple non-contact cases can pass, but pairwise tests observe zero or stale resultant forces because only one endpoint or one matrix cell was updated.
insights.guidance: Trace every C argument of the form &array[i], &struct.field, or T *out that the callee assigns through. In Rust, write back through mutable slices and update all paired state such as previous normal force, previous tangent force, and the output vector together. For pairwise contact loops, factor a local apply_contact(src, dst) and call it once for each observable direction; do not stop after updating only the second particle or only the first particle. The completed public loop must visibly contain two update blocks per contact when both endpoints are observable: one block for `p1 -> p2` using matrix slot `p1_idx * particles_size + p2_idx` and writing `forces[p2_idx]`, and a second block for `p2 -> p1` using matrix slot `p2_idx * particles_size + p1_idx` and writing `forces[p1_idx]`. The second block is not optional just because the first block writes an equal-and-opposite force; tests may inspect each endpoint and each previous-force slot separately. Swap the normal vector sign, relative velocity order, destination properties, force matrix slot, and output force vector for the reverse block. If the available helper takes the output vector as `&Vector` or previous normal/tangent values by value, inline the arithmetic in the public loop instead of calling that helper, because those writes would be lost. Each direction must recompute with swapped particle/velocity inputs, use properties for the destination endpoint when the C code does, use its own `src * count + dst` or `dst * count + src` slot exactly as shown by C, clamp normal force and tangent friction in the same order, write the normal/tangent slots back, then add the signed normal/tangent contribution to that destination output vector. Apply global forces such as gravity after contact accumulation if the C loop does so.

insights.title: Create fixture roundtrip files relative to the test crate
insights.trigger: Tests write a file, immediately read it back, use octal-like modes, or fail with FileNotFound/Permission denied in the generated crate.
insights.goal: Make write/read roundtrips target the same project-local path and permissions.
insights.constraint: Do not use stale absolute source paths or C-style octal literals without translating their numeric value correctly. Do not create a roundtrip file with permissions that prevent the same process from reopening it for readback.
insights.risk: The production logic can be correct while generated tests fail before observing it because the file was created elsewhere or with the wrong mode.
insights.guidance: Resolve test fixture paths relative to the current output crate working directory. Ensure the write path creates parent directories as needed, truncates or replaces stale files, writes all bytes, flushes/closes before readback, and translates leading-zero C modes as octal values. If the Rust caller passes a decimal value that originated from a C octal literal, preserve the intended readable/writable owner bits defensively: create with at least 0o600, for example mode | 0o600 on Unix, rather than using the raw decimal bits as the whole permission mask.

insights.title: Keep serialized tree read/write layouts identical
insights.trigger: A tree or node hierarchy is written to a file and later read back through header bytes, node type markers, active flags, byte lengths, or recursive read_node/write_node helpers.
insights.goal: Make the writer and reader agree on one complete on-disk layout and preserve the actual root node instead of rebuilding an empty placeholder tree.
insights.constraint: Do not implement write as lossy preorder bytes or read as only header parsing when the C logic stores active datapoints, node markers, distances, and children. Do not report file-open failure merely because the translated mode lacks owner read/write bits.
insights.risk: The file can be created and compile cleanly, but readback fails or returns an empty tree because header fields, write_datapoint/read_datapoint byte order, length fields, optional markers, recursive node shape, or file permissions disagree.
insights.guidance: Define one local binary format from the C evidence before patching either side: tag plus NUL, version, branch/path/leaf parameters, datatype, padding to the header size, then recursive node records only when the read path actually consumes them. Keep header byte offsets semantic and stable: if the reader interprets the next header byte after branch/path/leaf as datatype, the writer must store the datatype there, not a root-node marker or another convenience flag. Put root/node type information in the recursive node record or another reader-matched field, not by overwriting datatype; otherwise readback can silently create a tree with the wrong element type and later inserts fail with type mismatch. Keep absolute and relative buffer offsets consistent: if the reader stores the whole file including the header in `buf`, recursive parsing can start at `HEADER_SIZE`; if it stores only bytes read after the header, recursive parsing must start at `0`. Do not read past the beginning of a post-header buffer and then return NoInternal or Unrecognized for a file the same writer just produced. Open roundtrip files with create/truncate/write and owner read/write permission at minimum; on Unix combine any caller-provided mode with `0o600` instead of using raw translated decimal bits as the whole permission mask. Flush after writing the header/body, and only then let the read path reopen the same relative path. First satisfy the local reader contract before inventing a deeper payload: if the shown reader only validates header metadata and keeps remaining bytes as an opaque buffer, write the complete header and return success rather than serializing every in-memory field. Do not make a writer fail merely because optional internal pivot/root fields, support vectors, child placeholders, or recursive helper state are absent in a simplified in-memory tree; those fields should either be omitted under a header-only reader contract or encoded with explicit absent markers that the paired reader accepts. For each optional datapoint that is actually serialized, write and read the same active marker, byte-length field, id length/string, data type or shared datatype policy, data length, data bytes, and path floats. Avoid placeholder empty nodes after readback when callers later observe the root node; reconstruct the actual root node only when the local reader consumes node records.

insights.title: Preserve existing tree contents on append
insights.trigger: A tree, index, trie, heap, or node hierarchy exposes an add/insert operation that can be called multiple times before or after a file roundtrip.
insights.goal: Make repeated inserts accumulate data instead of replacing the existing root and losing earlier entries.
insights.constraint: Do not rebuild the root from only the newly inserted batch when the tree already has a root. Do not drop existing child nodes, leaves, metrics, or stored datapoints just to simplify insertion. Do not return NoSpace merely because the simplified Rust fallback has not implemented the C split path.
insights.risk: The first insert and write can appear to work, but a second insert or readback-then-insert loses the previously written data, returns empty search results, or makes later serialization inconsistent.
insights.guidance: Handle the empty-tree case separately. When the root is absent, create the initial leaf or internal node from the new batch. When the root already exists, insert into that existing node or append to a compatible leaf and update its logical count; never translate a second add as a successful no-op. For a conservative correctness fallback, a flat leaf containing old plus new datapoints is better than replacing the root with only the new datapoints or rejecting the append. If the C split/repartition path is too large to translate locally, grow the leaf Vecs beyond leaf_capacity and keep nbpoints equal to points.len() rather than returning NoSpace; retrieval and serialization tests prefer an overfull but observable leaf to a failed second add. Preserve the tree's datatype check and allocate per-point path state for the new points, but leave existing points and root structure intact unless the C algorithm explicitly rebuilds the whole tree from both old and new data. Do not require optional pivot/support-vector fields to be present before a write can succeed if the add fallback only maintains a flat leaf; the writer should use the tree datatype/header or explicit absent markers instead of returning an argument error. After readback, an immediate add must observe a valid existing root or an intentionally empty tree, not a placeholder node that rejects insertion.

insights.title: Fix roundtrip file openability before layout
insights.trigger: A test writes a project-local file, the writer returns success, and the immediate readback fails with FileNotFound, PermissionDenied, FileOpen, or an open error.
insights.goal: Ensure the same process can reopen the same path for reading before spending repair budget on deeper serialization changes.
insights.constraint: Do not diagnose the serialized payload or invent recursive helpers while the read path cannot open the file. Do not create a file with mode bits that omit owner read permission.
insights.risk: A writer can return success after creating a write-only file, and the reader may report that as FileNotFound or FileOpen. The next repair then chases the tree or binary layout even though the first blocker is file openability.
insights.guidance: Keep the filename relative to the output crate working directory unless the C evidence requires an absolute path. In the writer, remove or truncate stale files, open with create/write/truncate, combine Unix modes defensively as `(mode as u32) | 0o600`, write all required bytes, flush, and let the handle close before readback. In the reader, map an open error to the project's file-open error consistently, but first make the writer create a readable file. Once openability is fixed, then check header offsets, byte order, and optional node records.

insights.title: Keep gap buffers fully allocated to capacity
insights.trigger: Gap-buffer text storage tracks string length, gap length, gap location, split buffers, or character lookup around the gap.
insights.goal: Maintain the C invariant that the backing storage is addressable for the whole capacity while only non-gap characters are visible.
insights.constraint: Do not create a Vec with capacity only and then index it as if its length were initialized, and do not let split/move operations expose gap bytes as text.
insights.risk: The buffer can compile and insert simple text, but empty or split lines panic with slice bounds errors because gap_len reserves capacity without allocating initialized elements.
insights.guidance: Allocate the backing buffer with actual length equal to str_len + gap_len, filling gap slots with a placeholder value. Keep gap_loc within 0..=str_len, keep gap_len + str_len equal to buffer.len(), and when moving the gap rebuild prefix, gap, middle, and suffix so all slices are in bounds. get_string and char_at should read only the prefix before gap_loc and the suffix after gap_loc + gap_len. split should move the suffix into a new fully allocated buffer with its gap at the beginning and shrink the original visible length to the prefix.

insights.title: Normalize date sentinels before calendar indexing
insights.trigger: Date parsers use C tm fields, current-time defaults, mktime-style normalization, timezone offsets, microseconds, month/day arrays, or failures from indexing with -1/usize::MAX.
insights.goal: Preserve C approximate-date behavior while keeping missing fields and overflowed calendar fields out of Rust indexes.
insights.constraint: Do not index month/day lookup tables until tm_mon is known to be in 0..12 and missing year/month/day fields have been filled or deliberately rejected.
insights.risk: A parser can handle explicit dates but panic on time-only inputs or relative forms because C sentinel -1 becomes usize::MAX, or it can drop fractional seconds while normalizing calendar fields.
insights.guidance: Treat tm_year, tm_mon, tm_mday, tm_hour, tm_min, tm_sec, and tm_usec as semantic fields first, not indexes. After scanning tokens, fill missing date fields from the reference/current time before calling tm_to_time_t or mktime-like helpers; keep parsed time and microseconds intact. If a normalization helper must handle month overflow, adjust year with div_euclid/rem_euclid so the month is 0..11 before indexing month-day tables, then normalize day underflow/overflow by moving across adjacent months. Apply timezone offsets only after constructing the timestamp, and never cast a negative sentinel to usize.

insights.title: Store hash-table payloads with wrapping hash math
insights.trigger: Open-addressed hash tables initialize capacity, compute indexes, insert payload pointers, find values, delete last-found entries, or overflow in debug hash math.
insights.goal: Preserve both key lookup and payload ownership without debug overflow panics.
insights.constraint: Do not store only keys while dropping C void* payloads, and do not use normal overflowing multiplication for hash constants that C evaluates with unsigned wrapping arithmetic.
insights.risk: A table can find the key but then panic on an empty value, or fail before lookup because debug arithmetic overflowed.
insights.guidance: Allocate owned entry storage with explicit empty/deleted markers, key fields, and payload slots. Use wrapping_add/xor/mul for C unsigned hash formulas, compute indexes with the capacity mask when capacity is a power of two, and update last-found state on successful lookup if delete depends on it.

insights.title: Preserve collection equality through comparator fallback paths
insights.trigger: Set or collection operations combine membership, contains/remove, union, intersection, difference, disjointness, custom comparators, or byte-wise default equality.
insights.goal: Make every collection operation use the same element equality semantics for insertion, lookup, removal, and derived result sets.
insights.constraint: Do not require a compare callback when the C behavior falls back to raw byte equality, do not transmute a value into a wider destination, and do not drop the comparator when constructing union/intersection/difference results.
insights.risk: A collection can build successfully but later panic on a missing compare function, misclassify membership, or make derived sets disagree with contains/remove.
insights.guidance: Centralize equality in a local helper: use the supplied comparator when present; otherwise compare exactly the stored element width, using typed equality when available or safe byte-slice equality over size_of::<T>(). Carry the comparator and element width into result collections produced by union, intersection, difference, clone, or copy operations. Prefer callable-only fixes; if the only viable repair target is a whole impl block, preserve every existing public method that tests or callers can name, because cargo check can pass while integration tests fail to compile after a partial impl replacement. If a helper is defined inside the same generic impl, call it as Self::helper without adding an unnecessary turbofish; if hashing bytes locally, either use already-imported traits or avoid trait-dependent hasher methods in the patch. Avoid transmute_copy between differently sized types; copy only the bytes or typed value actually stored.

insights.title: Initialize open-address buckets with the probed empty sentinel
insights.trigger: An open-addressed set or map times out in insertion, probes bucket slots, and uses a signed marker field such as a probe index or distance to distinguish empty, occupied, and deleted slots.
insights.goal: Make the first insertion and every resize observe real empty buckets with the same sentinel that lookup/removal/probing tests use.
insights.constraint: Do not zero-initialize buckets when the probing loop treats a negative marker as empty; do not use capacity as the logical element count.
insights.risk: A table can compile and even expose the expected capacity, but the first insert loops forever because every zeroed bucket looks occupied.
insights.guidance: Define one bucket-state convention before implementing add/contains/remove: for example, empty/deleted when the marker field is negative and occupied when it is nonnegative. Allocate initial and resized bucket arrays by constructing explicit empty bucket values with that negative marker, then keep a separate logical size that increments only on new inserts and decrements only on successful removals. Every probing loop should either find that sentinel or stop after one full table scan and grow/rebuild instead of looping forever.

insights.title: Keep open-addressed set probing and equality state together
insights.trigger: An open-addressed set or map exposes add/remove/contains/iteration plus load factors, resize, hash callbacks, byte comparators, or bucket probe indexes.
insights.goal: Make membership operations, resizing, and derived set operations observe the same bucket state, probe sequence, and equality semantics.
insights.constraint: Do not replace C hash callbacks or double-hash probing with DefaultHasher plus simple linear probing when the C evidence has explicit hash1/hash2, seed, probe index, or load-factor resize state. Do not add Hash, Eq, PartialEq, Clone, or Copy bounds to generic public methods or impls unless those bounds are already present in the shown signature. Do not store an arbitrary signed cast of a hash in the occupancy marker when negative marker values mean empty or deleted. Do not panic, return empty, leave `unimplemented!()`, or skip membership work when the compare callback is absent if the C behavior falls back to byte equality.
insights.risk: The table may compile but most membership tests fail or hang because inserts land in different buckets than lookups, resize drops the old probe state, iteration drains the table, derived result buckets contain no empty sentinel, or default byte equality is treated as an error.
insights.guidance: Define one local equality helper and one local insertion path, then use them for add, remove, contains, iteration-backed operations, union, intersection, difference, disjointness, and resize. Keep every public method signature exactly as shown: for `impl<T>` methods, do not add `where T: Hash`, `T: PartialEq`, `T: Eq`, `T: Clone`, or `T: Copy` to make the code compile. Hash unconstrained generic values from their raw bytes with the shown C hash callback or a local byte hasher; equality must be total: call the custom comparator when present and otherwise compare exactly the stored element bytes with size_of::<T>(), not `PartialEq`. If helper logic is kept inside one callable, write valid Rust nested helpers: `fn helper<T>(...) -> ... { ... }` for named functions or `let helper = |...| -> ... { ... };` for closures. Never emit C-style pseudo declarations such as `helper(arg: Type) -> Ret { ... }` without the `fn` keyword. Avoid recursive closures for insertion/growth paths; use a nested `fn` with every needed state passed as parameters, or use an explicit loop/rebuild path. Use one identical hash/probe formula for insert, lookup, remove, and resize. Do not write separate simplified hash functions in add/remove/contains, do not change the secondary step formula between methods, and do not make contains/remove use a different seed or constants than add. For power-of-two bucket capacities, the secondary probe step must be coprime to capacity; use an odd nonzero step such as `(hash2 | 1) % capacity` with zero mapped to 1, not `hash2 % (capacity - 1) + 1` which can be even and cycle through only part of the table. If shared helpers cannot be added and keeping the probe formula identical is risky, implement contains/remove/derived membership by scanning occupied buckets with the same equality helper; a bounded O(n) scan is preferable to a mismatched probe that misses inserted elements, and scanning occupied buckets should be the default safe fallback for public set semantics. Initialize public sets with the C initial capacity and explicit empty buckets when capacity/init tests expect that shape; do not make `new()` or `init()` an empty Vec with capacity 0 unless the C API also reports zero capacity. For empty bucket arrays and resized arrays, do not use `vec![sentinel; n]` or `sentinel.clone()` unless Clone is already available; instead push a freshly constructed empty bucket for each slot, preserving the negative marker. Keep logical size separate from bucket capacity: size counts occupied elements, capacity counts slots, and loops over elements should scan occupied buckets rather than calling a by-index accessor with 0..size unless indexes are known to be dense. If the shared field name looks like bucket_size but capacity/init tests expect it to equal the number of allocated buckets, treat that field as capacity and compute logical size by counting occupied buckets or by a separate counter; do not repurpose the capacity field as the live element count. Preserve the bucket marker convention: negative or dedicated markers for empty/deleted, occupied markers for live slots. If the marker field is signed and negative values are empty/deleted, do not write `hash as i32` or any truncated hash into it; use a known nonnegative occupancy/probe marker such as the probe distance or 1, and store the full hash only in a separate field when one exists. After a successful new insert, the next size/count observation must increase exactly once; after a duplicate insert it must not change. Every probing loop in add, remove, and contains must be bounded by at most one full table scan; never write an unbounded `loop` that stops only on an empty sentinel, because derived or full tables can temporarily have no empty slots. If an add scans the whole table without finding a slot, do not recursively call add again at the same capacity; grow or rebuild into fresh empty buckets and retry with an iterative loop or return a real failure according to the C API. On resize or derived-set construction, rebuild every occupied element into freshly initialized empty buckets and update logical size separately from capacity. Derived result sets must not be represented as a dense vector containing only occupied buckets; allocate extra empty sentinel slots or insert each result element through the same add/equality path so later contains/remove calls can terminate on misses. A derived operation that writes directly into the first empty result bucket must first ensure the result has enough spare slots for all possible matches and must grow/rebuild before the slot scan is exhausted; never panic or return a dummy failure just because a reused result set previously had a smaller capacity. Reusing a result set for a larger union/intersection/difference must clear old markers, preserve configuration, then grow or call the common add path for each survivor so the new logical size can exceed the previous result size. If the public API only requires set semantics and not stable bucket positions, a simple coherent scan-plus-add rebuild is safer than mixing hash probes, copied probe indexes, and direct bucket placement. Iteration over occupied buckets should observe elements without clearing bucket markers, replacing buckets, taking ownership of the whole bucket vector, or decrementing logical size unless the C API explicitly consumes the set; for by-value iteration over C-like plain data, use a narrow pointer read of each occupied element and leave the bucket state unchanged, and a following contains/size call must still observe the same set. Derived sets must carry the comparator, element width, seed, load factors, and sentinel policy, and should insert through the same add/equality path to avoid duplicates. A compile fallback that leaves `unimplemented!()`, `todo!()`, `panic!()`, or a dummy success return in add/remove/contains/iter/union/intersection/difference/clear is not an implementation; repair the shared helper or callable instead.

insights.title: Copy bucket values without adding Clone bounds
insights.trigger: A bucket or vector accessor returns a stored generic element by value and compile repair reports a move from an index or a missing clone method.
insights.goal: Preserve C value-copy accessor semantics without changing the public generic bounds.
insights.constraint: Do not add Clone or Copy bounds to a public impl just to satisfy one accessor, and do not call clone when the stored element type is unconstrained.
insights.risk: A direct Rust move from an indexed bucket fails to compile; a clone-based repair also fails or changes the interface contract by requiring Clone.
insights.guidance: For an accessor whose C macro returns the stored element value from an occupied bucket, emulate the C by-value copy at that boundary with a narrow unsafe pointer read from the element slot. Keep the occupancy marker and bucket array unchanged, and use this only for by-value accessors, not for observing iterators that must leave elements owned in place.
keywords: does not implement the Copy trait

insights.title: Return mutable field accessors from shared receivers with raw field addresses
insights.trigger: A fixed public accessor signature returns a mutable reference from a shared receiver and compile repair reports invalid reference casting or borrowing behind a shared reference.
insights.goal: Keep the required interface while avoiding linted casts through an intermediate shared reference.
insights.constraint: Do not change the public receiver from shared to mutable, and do not cast `&field` to `&mut field` through a shared reference.
insights.risk: A direct borrow cannot compile, and a repair that casts `&field as *const _ as *mut _` is rejected by invalid-reference-casting lints.
insights.guidance: When the interface is fixed as shared receiver to mutable field reference, take the raw field address directly with core::ptr::addr_of!(self.field), cast that raw pointer to mut, and dereference it in one narrow unsafe block. Apply this only to accessor shims whose caller-visible contract already requires mutable access from a shared receiver; otherwise prefer a normal mutable receiver.

insights.title: Store sparse bitmap groups by rank, not dense index offsets
insights.trigger: A sparse array or sparse dictionary stores elements in bitmap-marked groups and computes get/set positions from group bit counts.
insights.goal: Preserve compact sparse storage and dictionary ownership while making absent keys and overwritten values observable.
insights.constraint: Do not store elements at `index * elem_size` inside a sparse group when the C code packs only occupied slots, and do not accept, truncate, or pad an inserted value whose byte length is larger than the configured element size when the C API reports failure. Do not keep raw pointers to temporary key/value buffers for dictionary buckets. Do not serialize, memcpy, shift, or drop Rust-owned dictionary buckets (`String`, `Vec`, `Box`, raw allocation pointers, or pointer/length pairs) as anonymous bytes inside a `Vec<u8>` sparse group. Do not invent a bucket owner type that disagrees with the shared bucket struct fields already shown in the prompt.
insights.risk: Basic set calls may appear to work, but get returns the wrong slot or dangling data once keys collide, many keys are inserted, an earlier sparse index is absent, value sizes differ, or resizing copies pointer-owning bucket bytes and corrupts the heap. A repair can also fail compilation if it stores Vec<u8> into a String key field, wraps buckets in Box when callers expect plain values, or calls a helper that was not actually defined.
insights.guidance: For each group, use the occupancy bitmap to compute rank: count set bits before the target position. Reject out-of-range indexes and reject values larger than the group's fixed element size before mutating the bitmap; only shorter values may be zero-padded when the C code does so. On insert, set the bit, grow the compact byte storage by exactly one fixed-size element, shift later occupied elements right, and write the new element at `rank * elem_size`; on overwrite, write in place at that rank without changing the slot width. On get, return None when the bit is clear and otherwise read the compact rank slot. Keep the generic sparse-array byte storage for plain fixed-width byte elements only. For dictionary buckets, store typed owned key and value bytes together with hash and lengths in a durable owner such as `Option<Bucket>`, `Vec<Option<Bucket>>`, or another dict-owned table; do not represent a bucket as raw bytes containing pointers, and do not reconstruct `Vec::from_raw_parts` from copied pointer fields. Match the shown shared item exactly: if the bucket key field is `String`, store a valid `String` derived from the key bytes or change every affected shared item and call site consistently; if the table field is `Vec<Option<Bucket>>`, do not return `Vec<Option<Box<Bucket>>>` unless all signatures and field types are patched together. If a resize helper is needed, define it in the same callable as a valid nested `fn` or patch a real shared helper; do not call an imagined `rehash`, `grow`, or `resize` helper by name. If a compact sparse index is still useful for the dictionary, let it point to or index typed owned buckets rather than owning their raw memory image. If a byte serialization is unavoidable, define one self-describing layout and use that exact layout in both set and get; do not write `[key length, key, value length, value, hash]` in one path and read `[hash, key length, key, value length, value]` in another. Do not change a sparse group's `elem_size` to each bucket's serialized length or mix variable-length records with the generic rank calculation; use a separate length-prefixed dictionary slot store or a typed owner for variable-sized values. Probing should compare key bytes and lengths before overwriting or reporting a hit. Probe until an empty slot is found or one full table scan completes; do not stop after `bucket_count` probes, because collisions can require more probes than the number of live entries before reaching the first empty bucket. After a successful new insert, increment the live bucket count exactly once; after replacing an existing key, leave it unchanged. When load reaches the resize threshold, actually allocate the larger bucket array and reinsert every occupied typed bucket through the same hash/probe path, moving owned key/value objects exactly once; do not byte-copy ownership records and do not leave a comment saying resize is omitted while still returning success.

insights.title: Use block ECC syndrome parity instead of byte XOR checksums
insights.trigger: Block error-correcting code encoders or decoders add parity bytes, correct one-bit errors, reject double-bit errors, or process fixed-size data blocks.
insights.goal: Preserve the C block-level ECC syndrome behavior for encoding and decoding rather than a checksum-only approximation.
insights.constraint: Do not implement the parity byte as a simple XOR checksum of the data bytes, and do not decode by blindly dropping every parity byte when tests or C code exercise single-bit correction and double-bit detection.
insights.risk: The output length can be right while parity bytes, corrected data, and double-error rejection are wrong.
insights.guidance: Model each fixed-size data block as individual bits plus a parity/syndrome byte. If the public encode/decode wrapper calls a helper named like an ECC/Hamming encode_impl or decode_impl and the helper body is not shown, inline the helper semantics instead of replacing it with a byte XOR checksum. Encoding should compute the same syndrome/parity bit positions as the C implementation over the block, append the block parity byte, and handle partial trailing blocks with the same reduced data length. Decoding should recompute syndrome, correct the addressed single-bit data error when the syndrome identifies one, accept clean blocks, and reject uncorrectable double-bit errors rather than returning corrupted data. Keep output sizing separate from correction logic.

insights.title: Decode Hamming blocks from position syndrome plus overall parity
insights.trigger: A Hamming-style block encoder stores one check byte whose low bits are an xor of logical bit positions and whose high bit stores overall parity.
insights.goal: Correct exactly one data-bit error and reject double-bit errors using the same syndrome/parity decision tree as the C implementation.
insights.constraint: Do not brute-force every possible bit flip until parity matches, do not treat a parity-bit error as a data-byte correction, and do not special-case literal test input/output byte arrays or one observed fixture.
insights.risk: Brute-force correction or fixture-specific branches can silently turn double-bit errors into plausible data, flip the wrong data bit while still matching the parity byte, or pass one encode assertion while failing roundtrip and error-correction tests.
insights.guidance: Use one shared data-bit to Hamming-position mapping for both encode and decode. Walk data bits in byte/bit order while incrementing a logical position counter and skipping Hamming parity positions 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, and so on before assigning each data bit its position. Encoding should xor those non-power-of-two positions for set data bits into the low seven syndrome bits, compute overall parity across data bits plus the low syndrome bits, and store the high check bit according to the C odd/even parity convention. Decoding should recompute the same position xor from the received data, xor it with `check & 0x7f`, and decide from that syndrome plus overall parity. If syndrome is zero, copy data unchanged. If syndrome is nonzero but overall parity says there were at least two errors, reject the block. If syndrome is a power of two, only a parity position is wrong, so leave data unchanged and accept. Otherwise map the non-power-of-two syndrome back to a data bit with `data_bit = syndrome - floor_log2(syndrome) - 2`, then flip only that addressed data bit when it lies inside the block. A byte-wise xor checksum or hard-coded known vector is never this algorithm, even if the wrapper helper body is not included in the prompt.

insights.title: Read compact random key tables through one bounds-safe helper
insights.trigger: A hash or polynomial multiply routine indexes a fixed random/key table using large byte offsets, key offsets, polynomial offsets, final-key offsets, or per-block key indexes.
insights.goal: Keep key-dependent hashing deterministic without panicking when the public key slice is compact or shorter than C's internal expanded table.
insights.constraint: Do not read key material with direct slice ranges such as `random[key_offset..key_offset + 8]`, `random[poly_offset..]`, or `words[index]` unless that exact range was proven in bounds for every input length. Do not return 0, `(0, 0)`, or a dummy constant when a polynomial/final/length key window is outside the public key slice. Do not turn the C internal expanded-table size into a Rust public precondition such as `assert!(random.len() >= RANDOM_BYTES_NEEDED...)`.
insights.risk: A hash can pass the example that uses a generated full key but panic on unit, avalanche, collision, or short-key tests with a custom compact key slice before hashing semantics are observed. If missing high key words are zero-filled, fixed byte offsets are read directly from a compact slice, or compact key bytes are folded into one u64 with shifts such as `byte << (8 * i)` for i greater than seven, short-key tests can panic, collapse every hash to 0, or make different late-block inputs hash identically.
insights.guidance: Create one local helper for all random/key reads, for example `key_word(index) -> u64`, before deriving polynomial, final, length, or per-block keys. The helper must be safe and non-degenerate for every index: read available little-endian bytes when present; when the requested word is outside the compact slice, derive a deterministic nonzero word from the compact seed bytes and the requested index by wrapping through available words and mixing with splitmix-style constants, rotations, and the index. If folding all compact key bytes into a u64 seed, either process eight-byte chunks, rotate/xor each byte, or shift by `(8 * (i % 8))`; never shift a u64 byte by `8 * i` when i can be 8 or larger. Do not zero-fill any missing key word, do not return 0 for out-of-range key reads, and do not use a formula such as `seed * index + index` that returns 0 for missing word 0. If only one or two u64 seed words are available, synthesize distinct key words for all later per-block, tail, polynomial, final, adjacent, and length-key indexes from those seed words; otherwise long messages can ignore later bytes and avalanche or distinct-input checks collapse. Use this helper for per-block keys, tail keys, polynomial keys, final keys, key-length words, adjacent key pairs, top-level functions, and hasher-stored keys. Fixed internal offsets such as polynomial/final/length keys are key indexes too: derive them from word indexes, not direct byte offsets into the compact public slice. For example, a fixed byte offset equal to `N * 8` names `key_word(N)`, not a direct slice read at byte `N * 8`; never special-case those offsets with direct fixed-window reads or `(0, 0)`/`0` fallbacks. If a generated loop tracks message progress in 64-bit words, convert to bytes before reading the message: byte offset is `word_index * 8`. Do not mix word counts and byte offsets in long-block paths, because a loop variable that has advanced by words but is passed directly to a byte-reader can re-read early bytes and ignore later blocks. For every full-block and remainder path, each message word after the first block must be paired with a distinct derived adjacent key word and folded into the accumulator; late-block or tail differences must not be invisible. If the public function accepts `random: &[u8]` or similar key material, accept any nonempty compact slice and make even empty slices deterministic instead of asserting an internal SIMD/precomputed table length. Do not leave any direct `random[...]`, `random[a..b]`, `keys[...]`, `words[index]`, generated-table length assert, expanded-vector indexing path, `try_into().unwrap()` on a fixed key window, or out-of-range zero fallback beside the helper, including in top-level byte-slice hash functions.
